name: Jamal Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, happy to help. I'll warn you, I go off on tangents. My partner Leila says I can turn a trip to the shops into a two-hour story.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm learning to run an excavator at the Pellow Ridge zinc mine, open pit. Right now I mostly load the smaller trucks on the waste dump, because they don't trust me on the ore face yet. The big skill is putting the load in the middle of the tray, and I still slop it to one side sometimes and the truck driver gets on the radio. Best part is the crew; we play five-a-side football on Thursday nights. Worst part is the 5 a.m. starts in winter when the cab heater's broken, which is always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, no need to panic, carry on. At work we'd joke about the robots not turning up. One of the guys would probably bring a cardboard robot to football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan works. Get good on the excavator, move to the ore face, get my pay up. Leila and I want to get married in two years, so boring is fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big. Keep training, keep saving about 250 a fortnight for the wedding. I'd keep using the AI app now and then, like I do to check my payslip, because the overtime maths is a nightmare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a nil-all draw. Not exciting, but you don't lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Leila's job feel different from yours in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. She's a bank teller, and even in the boring picture her branch is cutting tellers because everyone banks on their phone. Funny thing is, I'm the one in the dangerous job and she's the one who worries about hers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said boring is fine. Is there anything you'd miss if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Sometimes I think a robot doing the night shifts would be nice. But no, I'd take it. Boring and paid beats exciting and broke.

S0.say: I'd say good, no need to panic, carry on. At work we'd joke about the robots not turning up, and someone would bring a cardboard robot to football.
S0.think: Privately it means my plan works: get good on the excavator, move to the ore face and get my pay up. With a wedding in two years, boring is fine by me.
S0.do: Keeps training on the excavator and keeps saving about 250 a fortnight for his wedding. Keeps using an AI app now and then to check his overtime pay.
S0.feel: Calm, like a nil-all draw: not exciting, but no loss.
S0.quote: Funny thing is, I'm the one in the dangerous job and she's the one who worries about hers.
S0.fieldNote: He talks in football metaphors and stories, and is easy company. His partner's bank job is the one under pressure even in the quiet picture, which he finds ironic. The wedding in two years is his main planning anchor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and we should get ahead of it, but sensibly. Not the end of the world. That's what I'd say at football, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, I'd watch what the senior operators do. If Marco and Steph start doing the new courses, I'd follow them. I'm not going to be the first guy to jump, but I won't be the last either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep running the excavator and sign up for whatever the mine offers on the new systems, once a couple of people say it's worth it. I'd nudge the wedding savings up to 300 a fortnight. And I'd probably start using the AI tools more, maybe to help with the training modules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Like the coach is watching you and you don't know if you're starting next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's the person at work you'd worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Petar, on the water truck. Sixty-one, can't send a text. If the water truck goes driverless, Petar won't retrain, he'll just go home and sit in his garden. Actually, he might like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should pay for the retraining, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. The company's saving money, so they should chip in. The government too, because it's not just one mine. I don't think it's anyone's fault exactly, it's just how it goes.

S1.say: I'd say change is coming and we should get ahead of it sensibly, but it's not the end of the world. That's what I'd say at football.
S1.think: Privately I'd watch what the senior operators do and follow them if they start the new courses. I won't be the first to jump but I won't be the last.
S1.do: Keeps running the excavator and signs up for the mine's new-systems training once a couple of colleagues vouch for it. Raises wedding savings to 300 a fortnight and uses AI tools more for training modules.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, like not knowing if you'll start next week.
S1.quote: If the water truck goes driverless, Petar won't retrain, he'll just go home and sit in his garden.
S1.fieldNote: His instinct is to follow trusted seniors rather than lead, and he named Marco and Steph as his signals. He thinks retraining costs should be shared and doesn't really blame anyone. His worry for Petar turned into a joke, which is how he handles things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is serious and the government needs to get a plan out fast. Not doom and gloom, but proper help. Even I'd post about that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared for both of us. Leila's job would go first and mine soon after. Two years isn't enough for my usual move of waiting to see what others do. By the time I've seen what works, the game's over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Leila and push the wedding back, or make it a small one at her parents' place. Cut the car upgrade, cut eating out, put everything into savings. And I'd start looking at jobs that need a person on site, like the mine's emergency response team, even if it's less money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, I'd say. Lying awake stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the conversation about the wedding sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila would be fine with small, honestly. Her mum would not. Her mum has been planning for three hundred people since we got engaged. I'd let Leila tell her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at emergency response. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when something goes wrong underground or on the pit, you want a person. Maybe that's not true with AGI either. But I'd rather bet on that than on driving.

S2.say: I'd say this is serious and the government needs a plan out fast, with proper help rather than doom and gloom. Even he would post about it.
S2.think: Privately I'd be scared for both of us, with Leila's job going first and mine soon after. Two years is too short for my usual wait-and-follow approach.
S2.do: Pushes the wedding back or shrinks it to a small one at his partner's parents' house. Cuts the car upgrade and eating out to save everything, and looks at on-site roles like the mine's emergency response team.
S2.quote: By the time I've seen what works, the game's over.
S2.fieldNote: He saw clearly that his follow-the-seniors strategy fails when there's no time to watch. Two incomes at risk at once is what makes this picture hit hard. Even under pressure he finds the humour, here in his future mother-in-law's guest list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so let's plan. Company, government, all of us. No one's coming to save you, but no one should be left alone either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to watch for a year and then move. I think I'd be all right if I picked something in year two. Leila would have to move earlier, her job's closer to the computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd keep digging and watch what the experienced guys do. By year two I'd start a diesel mechanic apprenticeship, if the mine runs them, because someone has to fix the machines for a while. We'd keep the wedding but small, and save the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see the pitch, if you know what I mean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone has to fix the machines for a while. How long is a while?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea. Maybe until the robots fix each other. I'm not trying to win forever, I'm just trying to stay on the field another few seasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Leila do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's thinking about nursing. She says AI can do the bank stuff but people still want a hand held in hospital. If she went back to study, I'd carry the bills for three years.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to plan, so let's plan, company and government and all of us. No one's coming to save you, but no one should be left alone either.
S3.think: Privately five years is enough to watch for a year and then move. He'd be all right if he picked something by year two, but his partner would need to move sooner.
S3.do: Keeps digging and watches experienced colleagues in year one, then starts a diesel mechanic apprenticeship by year two. Keeps the wedding small, saves the difference and carries the bills if his partner studies nursing.
S3.feel: Anxious but able to see the way ahead.
S3.quote: I'm not trying to win forever, I'm just trying to stay on the field another few seasons.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits his style: one year of watching, then a move. He is realistic that mechanic work only buys a few years. He'd back his partner's switch to nursing by carrying the bills, a generous plan he stated plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off, plenty of time, let's be smart about it. Probably the same thing everyone says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that I'd probably wait too long, honestly. That's my worry with this one. I'd get comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the excavator, get onto the ore face, get married on the full three-hundred-person plan. Somewhere around year four or five, once others are moving, I'd look at retraining. I'd keep using the AI stuff more as it gets useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly because I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get comfortable. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila. She'd nag me. Or seeing Marco sign up for something, that'd do it. I'm a follower, I know that about myself, so I'd need someone to follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your future kids to go into mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn to fix things and talk to people, because I don't know what else will be left. Mining, maybe not.

S4.say: I'd say it's a long way off with plenty of time, so let's be smart about it. He admits that's probably what everyone would say.
S4.think: Privately ten years is long enough that I'd probably wait too long and get comfortable. That's the worry I have about myself in this picture.
S4.do: Keeps running the excavator, moves up to the ore face and has the full wedding. Looks at retraining around year four or five once others move, and uses AI tools more as they improve.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, mostly because he knows himself.
S4.quote: I'd tell them to learn to fix things and talk to people, because I don't know what else will be left.
S4.fieldNote: His worry here is about his own habits rather than the technology. He openly calls himself a follower and named his partner and a senior colleague as his likely prompts to move. He spoke about future children for the first time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Both our jobs gone and no time to watch and learn. What would help is the company running real apprenticeships on site, paid, so you can retrain without losing your wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the fun stuff. If the crew goes, Thursday football goes, and nobody counts that in the numbers.

headlineQuote: If the crew goes, Thursday football goes, and nobody counts that in the numbers.
portrait: Jamal Ibrahim is 27 and is learning to run an excavator at the Pellow Ridge zinc mine, still sometimes slopping loads to one side of the tray. He's engaged to Leila, a bank teller, and saving for their wedding, and he plays five-a-side football with his crew. He is pragmatic and calls himself a follower: he waits to see what senior workers do before moving. He's calm in the plateau, uneasy in steady change, alarmed when AGI in two years leaves no time to watch and learn, and anxious then uneasy as the timeline grows, with a diesel mechanic apprenticeship as his likely move.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because both his and his partner's jobs could go with no time to watch what works.
whatWouldHelp: Paid apprenticeships run by the company on site, so people can retrain without losing their wage.
